Error Sets: Error sets are declared with `error{...}` syntax. They define a set of named error values. Errors are values, not exceptions — they have no stack trace overhead until returned.
Error Union Inference: `!T` is shorthand for an inferred error set. The compiler determines which errors a function can return by analyzing all `try`/`return error.` expressions within it. No explicit set needed.
Merge Error Sets: The `||` operator merges two error sets. Useful when combining multiple error-returning functions. `anyerror` is the global error set that all errors coerce to.
catch / unreachable: `catch` handles errors from error unions. `catch |err| { ... }` captures the error. `catch unreachable` asserts the operation will not fail (panics on error). `catch 0` provides a default value.
try Keyword: `try` unwraps an error union. On success, it yields the payload value. On error, it returns the error from the enclosing function. Syntactic sugar for `catch |e| return e`.
Global Error Set: `anyerror` is the global error set containing every possible error. It's the supertype of all error sets. Use for error-agnostic code or when the exact error set is unknown at compile time.
Custom Error Sets: Define custom error sets with `const Error = error{ NotFound, PermissionDenied }`. Error sets infer from function bodies. Error union types: `Error!T`. Merge with `||`: `error{A} || error{B}`. AnyError for dynamic errors. The `!` before return type means any error. Use `anyerror!T` sparingly — prefer specific error sets.

Input/Output.exp: Input and output operations in Zig.

Install Zig: Zig can be installed via zigup, zigenv, package managers, or pre-built binaries from ziglang.org/download. The Zig compiler produces native binaries for cross-compilation out of the box.

# macOS
brew install zig

# Linux (snap)
sudo snap install zig --classic --beta

# Verify
zig version
zig help
zig init-exe: The `zig init-exe` command scaffolds a new executable project with a src/main.zig and build.zig. Use `zig init-lib` for library projects.

mkdir my_project && cd my_project
zig init-exe
# Creates: src/main.zig, build.zig, build.zig.zon
zig build run
Hello World: Zig's hello world uses `std.debug.print` for output. The `@import` built-in brings in the standard library. `!void` indicates the function may return an error.
build.zig Explained: The build.zig file is Zig code that defines how to build your project. It uses the standard Build API to configure executable, library, test, and run steps with cross-compilation targets.
Zig Version Manager: Zig is pre-1.0 and evolves rapidly. Use `zigup` or `zigenv` to manage multiple Zig versions. Each Zig version may have subtle language or standard library changes.

# zigup (cross-platform)
zigup install master
zigup use 0.13.0
zigup list

# Check current version
zig version
Build System Deep: Zig's build system is written in Zig itself. build.zig uses std.Build API: addExecutable, addLibrary, addTest, addRun. Targets define cross-compilation. OptimizeMode: Debug, ReleaseSafe, ReleaseFast, ReleaseSmall. Dependencies in build.zig.zon. Custom steps via b.step(). Options passed via -D flags. Build.zig runs at compile time — no external build tool needed.

Integer Types: Zig provides signed (i) and unsigned (u) integers from 2 to 65535 bits: u8, i32, u64, i128, u256, etc. Arbitrary bit-widths like u7 or i13 are supported with optimal machine code generation.
Floats: Floating point types: f16 (half), f32 (float), f64 (double), f80 (x86 extended), f128 (quad). Literals use decimal or scientific notation with optional type suffix.
Bool & Void: `bool` has `true` and `false` values. `void` is the empty type used for functions returning nothing or as a tag for inferred error sets. `anyopaque` replaces C's void pointer.
anytype: `anytype` as a function parameter accepts any type at compile time, enabling duck-typed generics. Each call site monomorphizes the function for the concrete type.
Type Coercion: Zig performs safe implicit coercions: widening integers (u8 -> u16), optional to error union, pointer to const pointer, single-item to slice. Narrowing requires @intCast or @floatCast.
enum & union: Enums define named constants with explicit or inferred integer tag values. Tagged unions combine a tag with variant payloads in a type-safe way without hidden fields.
Sentinel Arrays & Slices: Sentinel-terminated arrays and slices: `[:0]u8` (null-terminated for C interop), `[_:0]u8` array with sentinel. @ptrCast and @alignCast for conversion. Sentinels enable zero-copy interop with C strings. Also: `[*c]` for C pointers, `[*]` for many-item pointers.

const vs var: `const` declares an immutable binding; the value cannot be reassigned but may still be mutable via pointers. `var` declares a mutable binding. Both require explicit or inferred types.
Comptime Constants: `comptime` variables are evaluated at compile time. `comptime var` creates a compile-time mutable variable. Comptime blocks can execute arbitrary Zig during compilation.
Shadowing: Zig allows variable shadowing in nested scopes. An inner declaration with the same name temporarily hides the outer one. Shadowing is lexical and confined to the block.
Undefined & Default Values: `undefined` leaves a variable uninitialized (use with caution). Types like integers, floats, bools have no default. Struct fields can have default values. `@memset` zeroes memory.
Anonymous Bindings: Use `_` as a variable name to discard values. This suppresses unused-variable warnings and is required when you intentionally ignore a return value or loop index.
Shadowing & Blocks: Variables shadow outer declarations in inner scopes. Block expressions ({...}) create new scopes and return values. Labels (@label) for named blocks. Use blocks to limit variable lifetimes and scope. Shadowing is explicit — makes code clearer about redefinition.

if Expressions: `if` is an expression that returns a value. All branches must return the same type. Supports optional and error union capture syntax for concise unwrapping.
while with continue expressions: `while` loops can have a continue expression executed at the end of each iteration (before the condition check). Supports break/continue and optional capture.
for with Ranges: `for` iterates over arrays, slices, and ranges. Range syntax `0..n` creates an exclusive range. Supports multiple objects in parallel, element pointers, and index capture.
Labeled break & continue: Loops can be labeled with `:label` syntax. `break :label` exits the named outer loop. `continue :label` skips to the next iteration of the named loop. Useful for nested loops.
switch Expressions: switch is an expression that must be exhaustive. Supports ranges (...), multiple cases, enums, integers, and value capture with `=>` syntax for concise branches.
Inline Loops: `inline for` and `inline while` unroll loops at compile time. Required when iterating over comptime-known tuples or when the loop body must be comptime-evaluable.

Function Basics: Functions are defined with `fn`. Parameters are immutable constants. Return type follows the parameter list. Functions can be public (`pub`) or private. `!T` indicates an error-returning function.
Function Pointers: Functions have types like `*const fn(params) return_type`. Function pointers enable callbacks, dynamic dispatch, and polymorphism. Use `&function` to create a pointer.
Inline Functions: `inline fn` forces the function body to be inlined at every call site. Useful for comptime-only operations or when function call overhead must be eliminated.
Calling Conventions: `callconv(.C)` uses the C ABI for FFI. `callconv(.Inline)` forces inlining. `callconv(.Async)` enables async frames. `.Unspecified` lets the compiler decide. Default is `.Inline` except for pub functions.
Error Return Traces: Zig tracks error return traces that show the call chain when an error is returned (not thrown). This is a debugging aid with zero overhead when no error occurs. Disable with `-fno-return-traces`.
Nested Functions: Functions can be nested inside other functions. Nested functions capture their enclosing scope's constants and types. They are not closures (no runtime captures).

Multi-dimensional Arrays: Zig supports multi-dimensional arrays with `[rows][cols]T` syntax. They are stored in row-major order. Access with `arr[row][col]`. Can be iterated with nested for loops.
Sentinel Arrays: Sentinel-terminated arrays `[N:s]T` and slices `[:s]T` guarantee a terminating value at the end. `[:0]u8` is common for C strings. The sentinel counts as part of the array but not the length.
String Literals: String literals are `*const [N:0]u8` (pointer to sentinel array). They coerce to `[]const u8`. Multiline strings use `\\` continuation. Raw strings use `c"..."` syntax for C strings.
Format Strings: `std.fmt.format` and `std.debug.print` use format strings. Specifiers: `{d}` (decimal), `{s}` (string), `{x}` (hex), `{b}` (binary), `{e}` (scientific), `{any}` (debug). Pad with `{d:5}` or `{x:08}`.
Slice Operations: Slices support runtime range syntax `[start..end]`, `[start..]` (to end), `[0..len]`. `@as` can coerce arrays to slices. Slices have `.len` and `.ptr` fields. Bounds-checked at runtime.
Array Concatenation & Multiplication: The `++` operator concatenates arrays at compile time. The `**` operator repeats an array. Both produce new comptime-known arrays. For runtime, use `std.mem.concat`.

Many-item Pointers: `[*]T` is a pointer to an unknown number of T elements (many-item pointer). No length information. Often used for C interop. Index with `ptr[i]`. Must know bounds externally.
Pointer Alignment: Pointers carry alignment information in their type. `*align(N) T` specifies alignment. `@alignCast` changes alignment (unsafe). Misaligned access can crash on some architectures.
Slice Pointers: `[]const T` is a slice (fat pointer: ptr + len). Slices are the preferred way to work with contiguous memory. Syntax `arr[start..end]` creates a slice. `@as` coerces arrays to slices.
Allocator Types: Zig provides several allocators: `page_allocator` (syscall per alloc), `arena_allocator` (arena free), `GeneralPurposeAllocator` (heap), `FixedBufferAllocator` (pre-allocated buffer), `StackFallbackAllocator`.
Memory Leak Detection: GeneralPurposeAllocator can detect memory leaks on deinit. Enable leak detection with `.{ .enable_memory_limit = true }` or check `deinit()` return value which indicates leaks.
Comptime Pointer Handling: Pointers to comptime-known values can be created and manipulated at compile time. `@ptrFromInt` converts an integer to a pointer. `@intFromPtr` gets the address. Use with caution.

orelse & Unwrap: `orelse` provides a default value when an optional is null. `x orelse default` unwraps if present, otherwise returns `default`. Can also use `orelse return`, `orelse unreachable`.
if Capture: `if (optional) |value| { ... } else { ... }` captures the unwrapped value in the true branch. The captured value is a const binding. Use `if (x) |*ptr|` for mutable capture.
Payload Capturing: Optionals can be used with `while` loops to iterate until null. `while (iter.next()) |val| { ... }` captures the payload. Also works with error unions: `while (try iter.next()) |val|`.
Optional Pointers: Optional pointers `?*T` are size-optimized: null is represented as address 0, so no extra tag byte. This makes `?*T` the same size as `*T`. Useful for linked lists and trees.
orelse & Unwrapping Patterns: Optional unwrapping: `orelse` provides default, `.?` asserts non-null (panics if null), `if (x) |val|` captures, `while (x) |val|` loops until null. `x orelse unreachable` for invariants. `x orelse return` early exit. `x orelse continue` in loops. Nullable pointer interop via `?*T`. Compile-time optionals with `comptime`.

Compile-time Parameters: Function parameters prefixed with `comptime` are evaluated at compile time. Common uses: generic type parameters (`comptime T: type`), comptime integers for array sizes, and comptime booleans for conditional compilation.
Compile-time Variables: `comptime var` declares a mutable variable evaluated at compile time. `comptime` blocks execute arbitrary Zig at build time. Useful for generating lookup tables, assertions, and precomputed values.
@compileLog: `@compileLog(...)` prints values at compile time, useful for debugging comptime code. It outputs to stderr during compilation. Does not generate runtime code.
@field: `@field(lhs, field_name)` accesses a field or method by comptime string name. Enables dynamic field access at compile time. Pairs with `@hasField` for safe access.
@hasDecl & @hasField: `@hasDecl(comptime T, name)` checks if a declaration (type, fn, const) exists. `@hasField(comptime T, name)` checks if a struct/union has a field. Both return comptime `bool`.
Compile-time Reflection: `@typeInfo` returns a tagged union describing any type's structure (fields, decls, layout). `@Type` creates a type from `@typeInfo` data. `@typeName` returns the string name of a type.
Reflection & Type Info: @typeInfo(T) returns a std.builtin.Type struct for runtime reflection of types. @TypeOf(x) returns the type. @hasDecl, @hasField check members. @field access. @typeName returns string name. comptime iteration over struct fields for serialization. @tagName for enum names. These enable generic serialization, ORMs, and schema generation.

packed Structs: `packed struct` lays out fields at the bit level with no padding. Fields use bit-level packing. Use `u1`, `u4`, `u7` etc. for precise bit widths. Field order is guaranteed.
extern Structs: `extern struct` follows the C ABI layout for FFI compatibility. Has platform-specific padding and alignment. Use for interfacing with C libraries and binary protocols.
Zero-bit Types: Types with zero size include `void`, `comptime_int`, `comptime_float`, and empty structs `struct{}`. They occupy no memory but participate in type checking. Arrays of zero-bit types also have zero size.
Field Alignment: Struct fields can specify alignment with `align(N)`. Also use `packed` for bit-level or `extern` for C-style alignment. Use `@alignOf(T)` to query a type's alignment requirement.
Default Field Values: Struct fields can have default values. When constructing with `Struct{ ... }`, omitted fields use their defaults. `undefined` can also be used as a field value to leave it uninitialized.
Anonymous Structs & Unions: Anonymous structs and union literals can be created inline. Struct literals use `.{ .field = val }`. Tuple-like structs use `.{ val1, val2 }`. Anonymous unions use `@as(union(Tag), .{ .variant = val })`.

ArrayList: `std.ArrayList(T)` is a dynamically-growing array of contiguous elements. Supports append, insert, remove, pop, and iteration. Uses an allocator for memory management.
AutoHashMap: `std.AutoHashMap(K, V)` is a hash map with automatic key hashing. Uses `std.hash_map` internally. Supports put, get, remove, contains, and key-value iteration with an allocator.
BufMap: `std.BufMap` is a string-to-string hash map. Keys and values are `[]const u8`. Convenient for configuration parsing, environment variables, and text-based key-value stores.
BufferedWriter: `std.io.BufferedWriter` wraps a writer with an internal buffer, reducing system calls. Use `.writer()` to access the buffered writer. Flush with `.flush()` when done. Essential for file and network I/O performance.
File I/O: `std.fs` provides filesystem operations: open, create, delete, rename, read, write. Use `cwd()` (current directory), `openFile`, `createFile`, `readToEndAlloc`, `writeAll`. Errors are explicit.
Formatting: `std.fmt.format` is the core formatting function. `std.fmt.allocPrint` allocates a formatted string. `std.fmt.bufPrint` formats into a buffer. Custom formatters for user types via `format` method.
File I/O with std.fs: std.fs provides file operations: cwd().openFile, openDir, createFile. File.read/write, reader/writer helpers. Directory iteration with .iterate(). Path manipulation with std.fs.path. Temp files with tmpDir(). Atomic file operations. Memory-mapped files via std.os.mmap.

Async / Await Deep Dive: Zig's async functions use cooperative multitasking with no hidden runtime. `suspend` yields control. `resume` continues a suspended frame. Async frames are explicit values. Works with any event loop.
@cImport in Depth: `@cImport` parses C headers at compile time. `@cInclude`, `@cDefine`, `@cUndef`, `@cIncludeOptions` control the C preprocessor. Translate C types to Zig: `*c_void`, `c_int`, `c_char`, etc.
Inline Assembly: `asm` blocks embed architecture-specific assembly. Use `volatile` to prevent optimization. Output and input constraints use a declarative syntax. Useful for performance-critical or hardware-specific code.
Vectorization: Zig has built-in vector types: `@Vector(len, T)` for SIMD. Vectors support element-wise arithmetic and built-in reduction operations. The compiler auto-vectorizes where possible. Use `@shuffle`, `@reduce`.
@export & Section Attributes: `@export` makes a declaration available to the linker with a specific name, linkage, and section. Use for shared library exports, interrupt handlers, or placing code/data in custom linker sections.
Build System Advanced: The build system supports conditional compilation with `comptime` options, custom build steps, dependency management via `build.zig.zon`, cross-compilation to any target, and custom run/test configurations.
Inline Assembly (@asm): Zig inline assembly via `asm` expression. Syntax: `asm(volatile, "instructions", .(outputs), .(inputs), .(clobbers));`. Registers: [name] "constraint" (var). Constraints: "r" (register), "m" (memory), "i" (immediate). Volatile prevents dead-code elimination. No need for separate asm files — keeps everything in Zig.

Testing with zig test: Zig's built-in test system: `test "name" { ... }` blocks. Run with `zig test src/main.zig` or `zig build test`. std.testing provides expect, expectEqual, expectError, expectString. Test allocator (std.testing.allocator) detects leaks. Test runner: `zig test --test-filter "foo"`. Tests compile and run at full speed — no test framework overhead.
build.zig.zon Package Manager: Zig's package manager uses `build.zig.zon` to declare dependencies with URL and hash verification. Use `zig fetch --save` to add packages. Dependencies expose modules importable in build.zig.
Cross-Compilation: Zig cross-compiles out of the box — no SDK needed. Specify `-target` with triple: `arch-os-abi`. Supports x86_64-linux, aarch64-macos, wasm32-freestanding, and hundreds more. Build.zig uses `b.standardTargetOptions(.{})` for configurable targets.

# Cross-compile for ARM Linux
zig build-exe src/main.zig -target aarch64-linux-musl -O ReleaseSmall

# Cross-compile for Windows from Linux
zig build-exe src/main.zig -target x86_64-windows-gnu

# WebAssembly
zig build-exe src/main.zig -target wasm32-freestanding -O ReleaseSmall

# List all targets: zig targets

# In build.zig: const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
WebAssembly with Zig: Zig is a first-class Wasm language. Target wasm32-freestanding for WASI or wasm32-emscripten for browser. Zig outputs small .wasm files with no runtime overhead. Export functions with `export fn`.
C Interop Deep Dive: Zig has first-class C interop. `@cImport` parses C headers. Types: `c_int`, `c_uint`, `c_long`, `c_char`, `*anyopaque` for `void*`. Call Zig from C with `export fn` and `callconv(.C)`. Translate C headers automatically with `zig translate-c`.
Zig fmt & Code Style: `zig fmt` auto-formats code to canonical style: 4-space indent, opening brace on same line. Style guide: camelCase for functions/vars, PascalCase for types. Use `zig fmt --check` in CI.
Debugging Zig Programs: Use `std.debug.print` for logging, `@breakpoint()` for debugger breakpoints, `std.debug.assert` for invariants. Build with `-Doptimize=Debug` (default) for full debug info. Error Return Trace shows the call chain on errors. Use LLDB or GDB for step debugging.
Package Management: Zig package manager uses build.zig.zon (Zig Object Notation). Define dependencies with URL and hash. `zig fetch` downloads and updates hash. Declare dependency in build.zig: b.dependency(). Module exposes .zig files via .addModule(). Version resolution is manual (no semver solver). Packages are cached globally.

Allocators Deep Dive: Zig's unique approach to memory management requires explicit allocator choice. The standard library provides several allocator implementations: page_allocator (OS-level, simplest but wasteful), heap_page_allocator (wraps page allocator), c_allocator (libc malloc for compatibility), ArenaAllocator (fast, bulk-free, good for parsing/compilation), FixedBufferAllocator (pre-allocated buffer, zero overhead), StackFallbackAllocator (stack first, heap fallback). Best practice: use the simplest allocator that meets requirements. No allocator is universal — choose based on allocation pattern: many small allocations (ArenaAllocator), bounded work (FixedBufferAllocator), or general purpose (page_allocator with caching).
Custom Allocators: Creating custom allocators in Zig is straightforward — implement the Allocator interface: fn alloc(ptr: ?usize, len: usize, alignment: u29, len_align: u29, ret_addr: usize) ?[]u8 and fn free(ptr: []u8) void. The std.mem.Allocator interface uses a vtable pattern. Custom allocators enable domain-specific optimizations: thread-local caching, pool allocators for fixed-size objects, stack allocators for parser/frontend memory, or tracking allocators for debugging. The Zig standard library's Allocator interface uses a struct with function pointers — a manual vtable pattern optimized for performance.
Zig Pointers & Slices: Zig has a rich pointer system: *T (single-item pointer to T), [*]T (unknown-length pointer to T), []T (slice: pointer + length), *const T (pointer to const data), *volatile T (volatile pointer for MMIO). Slices ([]T) are the most common — they carry length information and enable bounds checking. Use ptr[0..n] to slice arrays. Zig has no null pointers — use ?*T (optional pointer) for nullable references. The @intToPtr and @ptrToInt builtins convert between integers and pointers for low-level work. Zig distinguishes between pointers to arrays (*[5]u8) and arrays of pointers ([5]*u8).
Comptime Memory & Types: Comptime in Zig isn't just for values — it works with memory and types too. comptime blocks can create types, allocate compile-time memory, and execute arbitrary code at compile time. @Type creates types from a reflection descriptor. @typeInfo introspects types at compile time. inline for and inline while unroll loops at compile time. Comptime enables zero-cost abstractions: generic data structures without runtime overhead, serialization frameworks that generate code at compile time, and type-safe builders. Comptime memory is freed after compilation — it doesn't leak into runtime.

File I/O & OS Operations: Zig's standard library provides cross-platform file and OS operations. std.fs module handles files, directories, and paths. std.os provides OS-specific syscalls. Key types: std.fs.File, std.fs.Dir, std.fs.Path. File operations: openFile, createFile, readAllAlloc, writeAll. Directory operations: openDir, makeDir, deleteDir, walk. Error handling uses Zig's error union type !void. Memory-mapped files via std.os.mmap. Environment variables: std.process.getEnvVarOwned. Command-line arguments: std.process.argsWithAllocator. Zig's file operations are safe by default — errors must be handled explicitly.
Networking & HTTP: Zig provides low-level networking via std.net module. std.net.StreamServer creates TCP servers. std.net.tcpConnectToHost connects to TCP hosts. The std.http module (Zig 0.11+) provides HTTP client and server. For production HTTP servers, the community provides zap and httpz frameworks (C bindings to facil.io/uWebSockets). Zig's networking is asynchronous using non-blocking I/O with std.io.poll. WebSocket support is available through std.http.WebSocket (basic) or community libraries. Zig's error handling makes networking code explicit and safe.
